shots.narration: One North American root can start violent seizures within an hour.
By the end, Doug sits under a tree in the rain, and the rain is only the start.
Water Hemlock.
The United States Department of Agriculture calls it the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America,
and the worst of it sits underground, in the thick roots.
The poison is called cicutoxin, and it goes after the brakes in your brain.
Your nerves run on two kinds of signal, the ones that say go and the ones that say stop.
Cicutoxin blocks one of the brain's main stop receptors, so the go signals keep firing and nothing is left to calm them down.
Here's the part that ruins dinner.
Water hemlock belongs to the carrot family, alongside the carrot, the parsnip, the celery and the parsley,
which is basically the whole bag of a supermarket soup mix.
Picture a family reunion where one cousin has a criminal record and looks a lot like everybody else.
People have confused it with wild parsnip, and the agriculture department says so plainly.
Doug read the words "carrot family" in his guide, ticked the box,
and made a big pot of soup.
Doug did not agree to this.
He agreed to soup.
Doug has died. Again.
That one at least had to be dug out of a marsh,
and the next one gets planted on purpose, right beside churches.
He ate it.
The Yew.
Almost every part of this tree carries poisons that can stop a heart,
and people have been planting it in churchyards for centuries.
The Woodland Trust estimates that the oldest yew in Britain, at Fortingall in Scotland, is between two and three thousand years old,
and other guesses run far higher.
Nobody can simply count its rings, because the middle of the trunk rotted away long ago.
The poisons are called taxine alkaloids.
According to veterinary toxicologists at Cornell University, they block channels in heart muscle cells
and scramble the electrical signals that keep the beat steady, which often ends in sudden death.
Farm vets see it again and again,
and in early twenty twenty-four, four beef cattle in New England were found dead over three days after reaching a yew.
One was seen eating normally moments before it went down.
Here's the problem.
The only part of the yew that isn't toxic is the bright red cup,
and the seed sitting inside that cup is toxic.
It works like a cherry jelly sweet with a poison pellet for a centre.
Doug ate a handful of the berries, seeds included, because they looked festive.
He said grace first, to be safe.
Doug has died.
The yew was standing there long before the church, and it plans to be there long after.
The next plant goes for the mind long before it bothers with the heart.
Deadly Nightshade.
Its berries are dark and shiny and, according to the United States Forest Service, sweet,
and the plant carries powerful alkaloids, including atropine and scopolamine.
Those two block a messenger chemical that your body uses to run its quiet, automatic jobs,
like making spit and sweat, slowing the heart and focusing the eyes.
Shut those jobs down and the body overheats, dries out and speeds up.
Doctors learn the result with a rhyme:
hot as a hare, blind as a bat,
dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter.
The worst part is the hatter, but the eyes go first.
The pupils grow from a pinhead to the whole coloured ring, like a camera opening its shutter as wide as it will go.
The story goes that ladies at the Venetian court dripped belladonna into their eyes for exactly this look,
since bella donna means beautiful woman.
Poisoning brings a racing heart, delirium and hallucinations,
and none of it is fun, just confusion, heat and a body that will not settle down.
Doug is fine.
He has spent the whole afternoon explaining his day to a hat stand, which he believes is the narrator.
The narrator had the counter ready,
and the next plant is one Doug can see from the highway.
Oleander.
California has an estimated twenty-five million oleanders planted along its highways and roadsides,
and every part of every one of them is poisonous.
They shrug off long droughts, which is exactly why they line so many median strips.
The toxin is called oleandrin,
and toxicologists compare it to digoxin, a heart medicine that is only safe in carefully measured amounts.
Each heart cell has tiny pumps that shuffle salts in and out,
and the rhythm of every beat depends on them.
Oleandrin jams those pumps, so the heartbeat slows down, skips and stumbles,
like a metronome on a piano while someone keeps nudging the arm.
But that's not the strange part.
The most famous oleander story is about campers who died after roasting hot dogs on oleander sticks.
In twenty twenty, two toxicologists actually tried it,
and the hot dogs picked up only a negligible amount of toxin.
On top of that, fresh branches thin enough to use as skewers were too weak to hold a hot dog.
The skewer story is probably a myth, but the leaves are not.
Traffic hadn't moved in forty minutes, so Doug reached out of the window and chewed a leaf out of pure boredom.
Doug has died.
So far, Doug has eaten every one of these plants himself,
but next, something else does the eating for him.
Secondhand.
Mad Honey.
More than two thousand four hundred years ago, a Greek army ate wild honey near the Black Sea,
and every man who ate it went down.
The general Xenophon wrote it up himself,
and the men who ate the honey lost their senses and could not stand.
They lay across the ground in such numbers that the camp looked as if the army had lost a battle.
Picture a hillside of dominoes, all knocked over at once.
Nobody had died by the next day,
and on the third or fourth day the men got up again, as if from a drugging.
The real culprit was the flowers.
In the eastern Black Sea region of Turkey, bees feed on certain rhododendrons,
and those flowers carry poisons called grayanotoxins straight into the honey.
Here comes the worst bit.
Grayanotoxins stop nerve channels from switching off,
which cranks up the nerve that slows your heart,
so the heartbeat drops, the blood pressure falls, and the room starts to spin.
A review in the journal Cardiovascular Toxicology says the symptoms usually last a day or two,
and that in humans it is rarely lethal.
Technically, Doug wasn't poisoned by a plant at all, but by breakfast.
Doug is fine. Eventually.
The honey was the bees' fault, and the next one is entirely the cow's.
White Snakeroot.
On the American frontier, a glass of milk could kill you.
Smithsonian Magazine says milk sickness killed thousands of settlers and farmers in the Midwest,
and nobody had poisoned the milk on purpose.
When a cow grazes on white snakeroot,
a toxin from the plant passes straight into her milk.
The cows themselves got what farmers called the trembles,
with shaking that was worst in the legs and muzzle,
and the people who drank the milk got milk sickness.
Here's the cruel part.
According to a Texas A and M University guide to range plants, sending the toxin into her milk protects the mother animal and poisons the young.
Every time the cow got milked, a little of the poison left her and went into the bucket the settlers drank from.
One glass of milk, and the cow did all the work.
In October eighteen eighteen, Abraham Lincoln's mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, died in Indiana,
and the National Park Service says it was milk sickness.
Scientists only published a chemical analysis of the plant's toxins in nineteen twenty-seven,
more than a century after the settlers started dying.
Doug noticed that the cow was shaking, and he decided she was probably just cold.
Doug has died.
Until now, Doug always had to swallow something,
and the next plant only needs his arm and a sunny afternoon.
One touch.
Giant Hogweed.
According to the Royal Horticultural Society, this weed can grow five meters tall or more,
and gardeners used to plant it on purpose because it looked so grand.
A basketball hoop hangs about three meters off the ground, so the hogweed clears it with room left over.
It was brought to Britain from the Caucasus Mountains in the early eighteen-hundreds,
and then it escaped the gardens and kept going.
Its sap contains furanocoumarins, chemicals that make skin extremely sensitive to sunlight.
Brushing against the plant can leave that sap on your arm without you feeling a thing,
and for a while nothing happens.
Except the sap has a silent partner.
The damage only comes when sap on the skin meets sunlight,
and King County in Washington State warns that the combination can cause severe, painful burns.
The same agency says the skin's sensitivity to sunlight can carry on for years.
So the real weapon isn't the plant at all but the sun, and the plant just hands it a target.
Doug brushed past one in the shade, felt nothing at all,
and then stepped out into a lovely sunny day.
Doug is fine. Indoors.
The hogweed needed help from the sun, and the next plant doesn't need help from anything.
Gympie-Gympie.
University of Queensland researchers describe this rainforest plant as one of the most venomous plants in the world.
With its big, soft, heart-shaped leaves, it looks like it would make a decent cushion.
The leaves and stems are covered in stiff hairs about five millimeters long.
Ecologist Marina Hurley, who studied these trees for years, says the hairs are partly made of silica,
and they work like tiny hypodermic needles that inject venom on contact.
Think of a glove knitted out of fibreglass insulation.
In twenty twenty, Edward Gilding's team identified the venom's pain toxins, the gympietides,
which fold into shapes like spider and cone snail toxins and hit the same pain-sensing targets in the nerves.
The sharp pain lasts for hours,
and painful flares can keep coming back for days and weeks.
And then it gets stranger.
According to Hurley, dried specimens collected more than a hundred years ago can still sting.
The plant has been dead for a century, and it still wins.
Doug is fine.
Doug will be fine in a few weeks.
He has circled a date on the calendar, and he flinches every time a page turns.
Every plant so far needed Doug to do something,
and the last one doesn't.
No touch.
The Manchineel.
Guinness World Records lists this as the most dangerous tree in the world.
It grows on Caribbean and Florida beaches, and it looks like a lovely place to sit.
The Spanish called it manzanilla, little apple,
but also the tree of death.
Its leaves, twigs, bark and fruit all hold a milky sap that can raise burn-like blisters on skin.
When it rains, water off the leaves can carry the sap onto anyone sheltering underneath.
Think of a garden sprinkler filled with something you would never water anything with.
Burn the wood, and the smoke can cause temporary blindness.
The fruit is worse.
In the British Medical Journal, a radiologist described biting one on a Tobago beach and finding it pleasantly sweet.
Then her mouth went peppery, the burning grew, her throat tightened, and swallowing became very hard.
Many trees are painted with red rings or carry warning signs.
Here's the strangest part.
Florida lists it as a state endangered species, with only about twenty known populations,
and these trees help shield the shore from storm winds.
The state would like it to survive.
For all that, deaths are rarely documented, and one medical journal calls them more legend than fact.
Doug sheltered from the rain under it,
made a fire from its branches to dry off,
and then ate one of its apples.
The tree did not need him to eat the apple.
Doug insisted.
As far as the narrator knows, nobody has tried all three in one afternoon.
Doug has died.
Again.
The cap sat under that tree all night and came out without a mark.
It has no skin, no eyes and no appetite,
so it was the only one dressed for the occasion.
Doug deaths: three hundred and ninety-six.
Every single one looked harmless to Doug.
